A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work by Weindel and Heckel. All 40 pages of v1 and 31 pages of v2, including their appendices, provide readable text, equations, figures and tables supporting a reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original evolutionary-search experiments, constructed code sizes, prompt and hyperparameter comparisons, throughput measurements and repeated-run results.

after.justification: V2 reports original code-construction experiments, graph-solver comparisons, reasoning and prompting ablations, component analyses and computational measurements.

M1.justification: The core greedy construction, island-based evolution, output-hash deduplication and reset scheme remain. V2 adds per-instance normalized-gap feedback to few-shot docstrings and implements summary, reflection and joint summary-code evolution variants with reasoning enabled or disabled (Section 5.2). These are procedural adaptations within the existing framework.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates binary deletion-correcting codes. V2 adds quaternary single-edit-correcting codes covering insertions, deletions and substitutions, searching lengths 6–9 and reporting results through length 11. Binary two- and three-deletion evaluation extends through length 18. Three-deletion evaluation and single-deletion checks through length 25 already existed in v1.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated OnlineMIS, ReduMIS and Gurobi comparisons, explicit Helberg–Ferreira construction results, and DoDo-Code for quaternary codes. V1 principally compares against VT sizes, Landjev–Haralambiev search results, a trivial lexicographic baseline and cited minimum-degree results. Random greedy existed in v1 Appendix J but now participates in the principal benchmark tables.

E3.justification: Main single-deletion searches change from a 400K-function limit with early stopping and 20K additional functions to 500K iterations. V2 introduces $120 inference-budget comparisons, a primary top-50 mean normalized-gap metric, and held-out evaluation of a function selected on search instances instead of per-length maxima across functions. Qwen3/Gemma 4 configurations and direct three-deletion optimization add further protocols; three-deletion testing itself is retained.

E4.justification: V2 adds extensive reasoning-on/off and code/summary/reflection/co-evolution ablations across Qwen3 and Gemma 4, plus individual removal of six heuristics from a discovered two-deletion function (Appendix F). Existing deduplication, graph-input, scoring and prompt analyses are revised. The GPT-4o mini comparison and random-greedy code-size distribution analysis from v1 are removed.

E5.justification: V1 already includes three repeated default runs, variability across islands and min-max ranges across discovered functions. V2 makes three seeded runs standard and reports across-run mean/min-max bands, including pooled 12-run and 9-run reasoning comparisons. Appendix A adds throughput mean ± SD over four measurement windows and run-level variability in computational costs.

E6.justification: Results are substantially replaced and expanded. For two deletions at length 16, v1 Table 4 reports a maximum of 204 across joint-search functions; v2 Table 2 reports 200 for its selected joint function and 215 for both KaMIS solvers. Changed selection and search conditions prevent interpreting 204 versus 200 as a same-setting decline. New results include quaternary size 40,604 versus DoDo-Code's 36,368 at length 11, and findings against reasoning and summary-code co-evolution.

T1.justification: VT equivalence was already argued in v1 Appendix H. V2 Appendix E substantially rewrites the proof into separate priority and lexicographic-order claims: a conflicting VT word can have equal or one-higher priority, replacing v1's equal-priority argument. This changes mathematical reasoning, not merely presentation. V2 Appendix C also adds verification costs to the retained exhaustive-search complexity analysis.

C1.justification: V1 headlines new best-known two-deletion sizes at lengths 12, 13 and 16 and previously unknown optimal constructions. V2 emphasizes a proof of concept and VT rediscovery, acknowledges known non-uniqueness of short optimal codes, and qualifies multiple-deletion superiority against stronger graph solvers. Compute allocation, harmful summary-code co-evolution, deduplication's importance and quaternary-code construction become central contributions.

C2.justification: V2 distinguishes VT complements from constructions outside every VT class and discusses rediscovery versus memorization. It adds explanations for reasoning and co-evolution failures, interprets joint optimization as regularization, and analyzes the contributions of discovered heuristics. The retained exponential-scaling limitation is developed into specific encoder requirements, limited theoretical understanding and potential use as short inner codes.

D1.justification: V2 adds model-specific hyperparameters, computational-cost tables, batching and prefetch settings, immutable-graph documentation and graph statistics. Appendix A revises evaluator allocation from two CPU cores to one and timeout from five minutes to 30 seconds. The code-access statement changes from a promised FunDCC release to a stated DistributedFunSearch release. Conversely, v1's extensive verbatim prompt appendix is removed.

R1.justification: V2 substantially repositions the work around scientific program discovery and inference-compute allocation. It adds discussion and citations concerning AlphaEvolve, ShinkaEvolve, OpenEvolve/CodeEvolve, classical graph solvers, DoDo-Code and low-redundancy deletion constructions. It also explicitly contrasts its distributed implementation with existing systems and develops the connection to inner codes, while pruning much of v1's broader application survey.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Method steps become numbered subsections, experiments are reorganized around correction tasks and ablations, Limitations becomes Scalability, and a Conclusion is added. Several separate appendices are consolidated, with much of the earlier hyperparameter evidence retained in condensed prose.

P2.justification: The presentation is substantially redesigned: solver-oriented comparison tables, cost-versus-gap plots with uncertainty bands, and computational-cost, hyperparameter and graph-statistics tables replace much of the earlier display structure. Overlap histograms, numerous prompt listings and several tuning plots disappear. The existing VT-equivalent function listing moves from v1 Figure 6 to v2 Figure 3.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical credibility. Its graph-solver comparisons expose limitations missing from v1's record-size claims, while selected-function held-out evaluation and repeated-run ablations provide stronger support for generalization and search-design conclusions. Appendix F also supplies direct evidence about discovered mechanisms. Removing detailed prompt listings weakens self-contained reproducibility, but the improved comparisons, uncertainty reporting and more carefully qualified claims outweigh that loss.
